write.desc: The logical language analysis proofs are written in: connectives, implication and its relatives, the quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists', and above all how to read, order and negate nested quantified statements. These ideas belong together because each builds on the last, and they end in the skill of negating a statement with several quantifiers reliably.

points.name: Statements and the connectives and, or, not
points.what: Tell a statement (true or false) from a question or an open sentence like 'x > 3', and work out the truth of 'P and Q', 'P or Q' (inclusive or) and 'not P' with short truth tables.

points.name: Implication: what 'if P then Q' claims
points.what: Know that 'if P then Q' is false only when P is true and Q is false, so it claims nothing when P is false (vacuous truth) and says nothing about cause; recognise the many wordings ('P implies Q', 'Q whenever P', 'Q if P').

points.name: Converse and contrapositive
points.what: Form the converse and contrapositive of an implication, know that the contrapositive is equivalent to the original while the converse is not, and give examples where a true implication has a false converse.

points.name: 'If and only if' and logical equivalence
points.what: Understand 'P if and only if Q' as both implications together, and what it means for two statements to be logically equivalent, checking equivalences with truth tables.

points.name: Necessary, sufficient and 'only if'
points.what: Translate 'P is sufficient for Q', 'Q is necessary for P' and 'P only if Q' into 'if P then Q', and avoid the common reversal of 'only if'.

points.name: Negating compound statements
points.what: Negate 'and', 'or' and 'if ... then' statements mechanically with De Morgan's laws, double negation, and the rule that 'not (if P then Q)' is 'P and not Q', and say the result in plain words.

points.name: The quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists'
points.what: Read and write statements with 'for all' and 'there exists' (and their symbols), always naming the domain, and see how the truth of a quantified statement can change when the domain changes (for example integers versus natural numbers).

points.name: Translating mathematical sentences into quantified form
points.what: Turn everyday mathematical sentences into quantified form: spot hidden quantifiers ('if n is even then n^2 is even' means for all n), read 'every', 'any', 'some', and write restricted quantifiers such as 'for all x > 0' as 'for all x, if x > 0 then ...' and 'there is x > 0 with ...' as 'there is x with x > 0 and ...'.

points.name: Negating a single quantifier
points.what: Negate quantified statements: 'not for all' becomes 'there exists ... not', and 'not there exists' becomes 'for all ... not', including restricted quantifiers, and see that a counterexample is exactly a witness for the negation of a 'for all' statement.

points.name: Nested quantifiers and why their order matters
points.what: Read statements with two or more quantifiers, understand that in 'for all x there exists y' the choice of y may depend on x, and explain why 'for every x there is y with y > x' is true for integers while 'there is y with y > x for every x' is false.

points.name: Negating nested quantified statements
points.what: Push 'not' through a chain of three or four quantifiers step by step, flipping each quantifier and negating the final condition (including any implication inside it), then state the negation in clear words and check it against an example.

points.name: Reading 'for all ... there exists ... such that for all ...' statements
points.what: Read and negate statements of the shape used later for limits, such as 'for every k there is N such that for all n >= N, n^2 > k' or 'for every k there is n with a_n > k', and say in words what the statement and its negation mean (eventually above every bound, not bounded, and so on), without any epsilon definitions.
